articles.title: Why has France struggled to address students’ demands?
articles.summary: Protesters demand more spending on education and social services, but the government has struggled amid a fiscal crisis.
articles.body:
Young people in France continued their nationwide protests over the weekend, demanding better education facilities and a promising future amid the rising cost of living in the country.

France’s Ministry of Interior said 410,000 people protested nationwide on Saturday, including 110,000 in Paris, as the government has struggled to address the issues raised by the student-led protests.

France was also roiled by nearly two years of protests beginning in 2018 over the high cost of living and opposition to French President Emmanuel Macron’s economic policies. Those protests, which were led by the Yellow Vests movement , demanded that the government address the rising economic inequality, boost welfare and public services, and tax the rich.

As the young protesters take to the streets, many of the old demands remain unfulfilled. So, why have French politicians been unable to address the issues facing the country?

Why are young people in France protesting now?

The youth-led protests in France erupted last month amid deteriorating conditions in schools, broader economic anxieties and opposition to government budget cuts.

The protests began in mid-September after high school students blockaded campuses over overcrowded classrooms (often 32–35 pupils per room), unreplaced teacher absences, and dilapidated building infrastructure.

Protesters have waved placards reading statements like “We have a future to build, not to endure”, as they expressed frustration with shrinking public resources and state investment.

Teachers have also joined the students protesting over low salaries. French teachers are paid less on average than their counterparts in other European countries like Germany, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Education at a Glance 2026 report.

School teachers in France earn a gross salary of 41,968 euros ($46,900) per annum compared with 69,453 euros ($77,700) for their German counterparts. Social taxes, high pension contributions and the rising cost of living eat into their monthly income.

What started as a localised strike over school resources has since drawn in trade unions as well as civil servants, and the protests have evolved into a broader economic and political crisis.

This is due to discontent over the government’s proposed 54-billion-euro ($60bn) package of cost-cutting and tax measures for the 2027 budget, which includes civil servant salary freezes.

Students and youth fear bearing the brunt of public spending reductions amid a multidecade high in poverty rates and rising costs of living, exacerbated by the United States-Israel war on Iran.

Currently, according to Amine Snoussi, a journalist for Le Media TV and a former parliamentary assistant at the French National Assembly, the condition of public high schools is dire since government money is being spent elsewhere.

“Students are studying in cold, dirty buildings, some of them infested with rats. In some schools, absent teachers haven’t been replaced for over six months. And all of this is happening while thousands of teaching jobs are being cut, and while public money keeps flowing to private schools. That’s what lit the fuse,” he told Al Jazeera.

What has been the government’s response?

The French government has responded to the mass protests by imposing curfews and deploying police across the country to crack down on protesters.

President Macron has blamed ultra-left groups for trying to “bring down the Republic” and threatened accountability for those involved in violence.

On Friday, the French leader met representatives of the student movement for the first time since the protests began.

But the meeting failed to defuse tensions, with student representatives calling for further mobilisation until the government presents concrete actions.

On Monday, during a visit to Marseille, Macron said he has “asked the government to address the legitimate demands at the root of this protest movement”.

The government is also expected to announce changes to Parcoursup, France’s national online university admissions platform, according to French media reports.

Why is the French government struggling to address protesters’ demands?

Analysts say the French government is struggling to address students’ demands due to a severe fiscal crisis and planned budget cuts, which have led to a drop in the country’s education budget.

According to data published by French economist and co-director of the World Inequality Lab Lucas Chancel, “The public budget for higher education, student life, and research (relative to the total number of students in France, once inflation is taken into account) has decreased by 20 percent since 2017.”

The French government has defended the budget cuts.

In an address to the nation on October 7, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu acknowledged that “the anger among young people didn’t come out of nowhere” and promised the government would present a plan to address the crisis by the end of October.

The French prime minister has also asked his ministers to check spending as France’s national debt has ballooned to about 3.6 trillion euros ($4 trillion), which is equivalent to 119 percent of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP).

Of greater concern to markets than the total debt is France’s growing deficit, however, which is expected to reach 5.4 percent of GDP in 2026 – far above the European Union average of just more than 3 percent. This is the amount by which a government’s spending exceeds its income.

But in a report, French economist and professor Thomas Piketty noted that while public debt has increased, the country’s private wealth has also grown from “300 percent to 600 percent of GDP, with extreme concentration among the wealthiest financial fortunes”.

“In other words, France has never been richer. The problem to solve is simply one of distribution,” he added.

Does France have a wealth distribution problem?

France has relatively low to moderate income inequality, but wealth redistribution has been an issue of debate, particularly in left-wing political groups.

People aged 60 and older, who form a quarter of the population, own 60 percent of the country’s wealth (non-financial and financial), according to a January 2026 review by prominent French economic policy think tank OFCE.

A huge chunk of government funds go to service social security.

A government report seen by the Reuters news agency earlier this month also noted that nearly one-third of some French ministries’ budgets pay for the pensions of retired civil ‌servants, which reduces spending on education and other priorities.

Snoussi told Al Jazeera that the wealth distribution question has always been central to current French politics.

“Macron is called the rich people’s president for a reason. He always supports rich people and has never managed to create a form of equality between classes,” he said.

Macron has been branded “the president of the rich” for cutting the wealth tax. He has also faced criticism for his economic policies aimed at modernising the economy and creating jobs. His decision to impose a fuel tax triggered the 2018 so-called Yellow Vests protests, a grassroots movement seeking government intervention to address inequality.

Critics say his policies resulted in redistribution of wealth upward and affected the working-class population. But Macron has defended his policies, particularly his decision on wealth tax, saying that forcing the wealthy out of the country won’t help the poor.

“I don’t believe in this French jealousy which says, ‘There are rich people; let’s tax them and we will all feel better,’” he told The New York Times in a 2017 interview.

Antonio Fatas, a professor of economics at INSEAD in Fontainebleau, France, told Al Jazeera: “France has a more redistributive system than other European countries – at least similar”.

He explained that redistribution is a set of programmes of taxes and transfers that redistribute income from high-income individuals towards lower-income individuals.

“France’s growth has been limited for years. With low growth, it is not hard to imagine parts of the population that are unhappy with the progress they see, and this leads to demands for a solution in the form of government support or redistribution,” he said.

France is currently facing significant fiscal stress, with its annual budget deficit forecast at 5.4 percent of its GDP, well above the standard European Union ceiling of 3 percent. The country also remains heavily backed by its public sector, with state expenditures consuming roughly 57 percent of its total GDP – including a notable 14 percent allocated strictly towards worker pensions.

“The assumption is that someone out there is rich enough that they can be taxed. While I can imagine in a more progressive system in France, one has to be careful about the limitations of these apparent solutions,” Fatas added.

In his opinion column for the French newspaper Le Monde, Piketty wrote that reinvesting in sectors like education and health should be the government’s priority.

“Reinvesting in these sectors today is not simply a matter of equality between regions or social classes,” he wrote, highlighting that such reinvestment would help an economy produce greater output by using fewer resources.

“The government has a simple choice: invest, or step aside,” he said.

“But the real question is whether Macron even wants a way out. Or is he hoping the situation gets worse, so he can crush the movement through police and judicial repression?”

Fatas, the economics professor, noted that while there are a lot of good things people in France want the government to do, it is important to prioritise which sector requires funding.

“The government spending [in France] is the largest among advanced economies, so there is little room to just spend the way out of this.

“France faces a political paralysis when it comes to reform decisions, and this is the reason why they are in a more difficult situation than others,” he added.

articles.title: A Wyoming landowner claimed a conservation group promised he could build a guest house without a kitchen; federal appeals court rejected his claim
articles.summary: A Wyoming landowner’s attempt to build a second residential structure on conservation land led to years of litigation with The Nature Conservancy (TNC).
articles.body: A Wyoming landowner’s attempt to build a second residential structure on conservation land led to years of litigation with The Nature Conservancy (TNC). Gary Binning wanted to build a guest house on property subject to a conservation easement, which restricted construction to one single-family residential structure per parcel.After losing an earlier case before the Wyoming Supreme Court, Binning said TNC’s state director had orally agreed he could build a structure for overnight guests if it was not called a guest house and had no kitchen.According to the US Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit dated 15 April 2026, the court rejected Binning’s appeal, finding that the alleged promise was not sufficiently clear and that relying on it was unreasonable. The ruling upheld the district court’s judgment in favour of TNC.Wyoming landowner faced restrictions on guest house construction on 500-acre ranchThe dispute began with a 500-acre Wyoming ranch between the Snake River and Grand Teton National Park. A conservation easement was established on the land to protect its natural, scenic, or open-space values. The easement allowed an owner to construct one additional single-family residential structure on each subdivided parcel, alongside associated improvements.In an earlier case, the Wyoming Supreme Court interpreted that wording as permitting only one building in which one family could live. It ruled that associated improvements did not include another residential structure, such as a guest house or caretaker’s quarters.Guest house dispute centred on an alleged promise by TNC directorAfter the Wyoming Supreme Court ruling, Binning continued seeking a way to accommodate overnight visitors. He and his wife, Marianna, later met TNC’s Wyoming state director, Hayley Mortimer, for lunch in Jackson. Binning testified that Mortimer wanted to resolve the dispute and said he could build a structure if he did not call it a guest house, left out a kitchen, and followed Teton County’s Land Development Regulations.Marianna also recalled similar comments. Mortimer did not remember making the alleged promise. She said she had told Binning that she needed to consult the organisation’s lawyers and qualified staff before following up. Her later letter described the meeting as a request for additional guidance about the property’s development at that stage.A kitchenless design failed to resolve the Wyoming building disputeIn her letter after the lunch, Mortimer said TNC would not object to a design if Teton County approved it as one single-family residential structure rather than multiple accessory residential units. Binning sought changes to the letter but did not refer to the alleged lunchtime promise in his response. He later asked his architects to design a “kitchenless wellness centre” where guests could stay overnight.Teton County approved permits for three buildings in July 2022, including a gym and yoga studio with about 2,500 square feet of habitable space. TNC rejected the wellness centre plans, pointing to four rooms with adjoining bathrooms, laundry facilities and food-preparation features.Appeals court rejected landowner’s claim over alleged verbal promiseBinning sued, arguing that promissory estoppel should prevent TNC from blocking the building. Under Wyoming law, the claim required a clear and definite promise, reasonable reliance that caused detriment, and a finding that enforcement was necessary to avoid injustice. The Tenth Circuit said the lunch comments were conditional and did not represent a definite commitment.It also found reliance unreasonable because Binning had years of litigation behind him, wanted written confirmation, and knew the alleged oral agreement conflicted with the Wyoming Supreme Court ruling. TNC’s follow-up letter did not confirm the promise, and Binning’s correspondence did not mention it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Shopkeeper in Catford immortalised by royal portrait artist
articles.summary: Artist Nick Bashall depicts Kaual Patel, owner of Torridon Convenience Store in Catford.
articles.body:
A corner shop owner from south London has been painted by a royal portraitist in a project to recognise the impact of independent businesses in their local communities.

Artist Nick Bashall, who painted Princess Anne, has depicted Kaual Patel, owner of Torridon Convenience Store in Catford.

The work will be revealed to the public in a new exhibition, Local Royalty, alongside paintings by other royal artists of pub, cafe and takeaway owners.

The event was inspired by research that indicated nearly 80% of the public believed independent businesses such as corner shops are underappreciated.

The exhibition depicts Patel alongside three other small business owners who have been immortalised in a manner historically reserved for royalty, titans of industry and stars of stage and screen.

He took over the shop from his father and uncle and has spent the past two decades creating a hub for the local community and championing local producers.

"The days I spent being painted by Nick, live in the shop, were unforgettable, but what made it truly special was seeing it through the eyes of my customers," said Patel.

"This wasn't created behind closed doors in a studio.

It happened right here, in the store, surrounded by the people who make our community so special.

Seeing their expressions, hearing their reactions and watching the portrait come to life alongside them created memories I'll never forget.

"This simply doesn't happen to an everyday shopkeeper."

Bashall said: "I stood at my easel and painted Kaual and the entire background on the spot, with people milling around us.

"It was great fun watching his customers' faces as they came in, clearly wondering what was going on, but also intrigued by it all."

The exhibition, sponsored by Coca-Cola GB, will be open to the public from 28 October to 2 November at the Saatchi Gallery in London.

articles.title: Cumbria's storm-hit families keep 'brave face' without power
articles.summary: Thousands of families start half term with camping stoves and candlelit dinners during Storm Boelo.
articles.body:
It was an unusual start to half term for thousands of families who were left without power during and after Storm Boelo.

Many communities across Cumbria resorted to camping stoves and candlelit dinners as high winds battered the county at the weekend, while food vans provided free meals to those worst hit.

Katherine Ord and her four-year-old daughter Eden, from Scotby near Carlisle, lost power on Saturday afternoon and slept with two duvets each to keep warm.

She said: "It's not ideal, but storms can't be helped, we do appreciate that. We're trying to keep a brave face." SP Electricity North West (ENW) told her power was expected to be back by Tuesday evening in the "worst-case scenario".

Ord said: "It's quite a long time, it's four days without any form of electricity. The novelty does seem to wear off a bit.

"The weather [on Sunday] was still really stormy and so we do appreciate that people are probably trying their best under the conditions and they can't be blamed, it still doesn't make it any easier at the time."

Her local supermarket cafe offered £1 meals for children, while neighbours who still had power helped with charging devices.

SP ENW said it struggled to reconnect customers on Sunday due to high winds which made it unsafe for staff to climb poles safely.

The company set up a welfare hub near Penrith and two in Wigton in the north of the county, as well as four more in south Cumbria.

Paul Killilea said the hubs were set up "on a case by case basis" in facilities such as cafes and pubs, but SP ENW also used mobile food vans.

One such van was at Bowscar, near Penrith, on Monday, where Seb Flint relied on it for warm food and drinks after his power went off early on Saturday.

He said trying to carry on with day-to-day tasks, such as working from home and accessing hot water, had been the biggest challenge.

"We're lucky we've got a little log burner so keeping the house warm's been all right. But obviously the worry about stuff in the freezer and when's [the electricity] going come back on."

Ewan Adair, who runs the Primal Feast van which provided meals to affected people, said: "SP ENW have door knockers, so they come to me in their vans, collect hot foods and they run them out to the people that can't make it over here."

Killilea said: "We've also proactively called more than 7,500 customers to offer tailored support and communication and are sending teams of door knockers out to those we have been unable to contact by phone or who need additional support."

articles.title: Billingham volunteers aim to sew 1,200 years of history
articles.summary: The Friends of St Cuthbert’s Church are recreating Billingham's timeline in embroidery.
articles.body:
Volunteers are working on an embroidered timeline to record a town's 1,200-year history.

The Friends of St Cuthbert's Church, Billingham, commissioned six panels depicting the "tiny little church on the hill" in the 9th century, through to the town's industrialisation and the influx of people coming to work in shipbuilding and chemicals.

Volunteer Jackie Ward said the story remained relevant because "without the economic migrants, the town really wouldn't have become what it is now".

Artist Harriet Mee said trying to fit hundreds of years of history into the designs was "quite a tall order", but she was honoured to be trusted with the job.

The charity is taking ownership of St Cuthbert's Church from the Church of England following proposals to close it due to costs and falling attendance .

Twelve volunteers of "all ages and skills" had already been working on the panels for a couple of months and it is hoped it will be completed by April.

"They're already learning things that they've never done before," Ward said, including applique, sewing and learning to upscale designs.

Mee, who is a freelance artist based in Stockton, said the first three panels depicted the historical origins of the area from Anglo-Saxon times in 850 AD and showcased a wild landscape eventually being cultivated for farming.

"Panel four feels so different because it's the introduction of the rapid industrialization of our area."

Ward said: "From 1801 we had 926 people living in the area and by 1961 we had 32,000.

"That huge thing was due to the influx of people who were economic migrants for the likes of ICI, the shipyards."

Mee said she had tried to stay true to local landmarks by using archive images when designing the skyline.

The sixth and final panel envisioned a "cleaner and more sustainable future", full of wildlife and featuring windfarms off the coast, she said.

Ward said the work was appropriate in "this year of the Bayeux Tapestry" coming to the UK.

"We're very quick to pull areas down and say the town centre's rubbish, the unemployment, the houses, and what not," she said.

"But at the end of the day we've still got an awful lot to be proud of and we need to continue reminding ourselves on that."

There hopes the panels will be exhibited at Billingham Library before being displayed in the church.

articles.title: Palestinian citizens of Israel fear they’re next target if far-right wins
articles.summary: Majd al-Krum’s protests have forced settlers to withdraw, but fears of further provocations loom after elections.
articles.body:
Majd al-Krum, Israel – The police closed the road to al-Rus, so the villagers found other ways up there.

Beginning on September 13, local Palestinian citizens of Israel made the steep climb to the pine-covered hilltop above Majd al-Krum using horses, off-road vehicles and on foot. A couple of weeks earlier, settlers from the occupied West Bank had begun building an outpost there, on village land – one of the first such attempts on this side of the Green Line, the name used for the boundary between Israel and the occupied West Bank.

The young Israeli settlers said they were there to graze livestock with a Jewish National Fund (JNF) permit. But there was no livestock, noted Hussein Mannaa, 50, a lawyer and member of the town’s Popular Committee. Within a week, the camp had grown from a handful of people to between 25 and 30, according to villagers, with a kitchen, a toilet, a water line and electricity.

Villagers rushed to the scene, so police closed the road to the site. Yet local Palestinians came in droves nonetheless.

Anas Sgaier, a 21-year-old law student and youth organiser, made the nearly hour-long climb up the mountain. “I remember one moment: I’m going up and it’s hard for me to breathe,” he said. “And to my right, I saw an older woman, in her 80s, with her husband … walking up 50 minutes, just to show her presence.”

After almost a week of peaceful protests that saw hundreds of Palestinians from Majd al-Krum and across the region come every day, the JNF ordered the settler tents removed. By September 16, the site was cleared out.

A little more than a month later, Israelis head to the polls on Tuesday, and Palestinian villagers fear al-Rus was a prelude to what may come next. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich is campaigning on a promise to “Judaise” the Galilee, where Palestinian citizens of Israel make up a large proportion of the population, and says he will repeat there “the revolution we carried out in [the occupied West Bank]”.

“The al-Rus experiment is like a pilot … experiment: ‘come on, let’s see the reaction’,” said Husein Khalaily, 50, an economic consultant, while sitting at his home in Majd al-Krum.

Reaction was swift: the village’s Popular Committee met as soon as the rumours of the settler outpost were confirmed and, with the local council, called daily demonstrations. “The popular struggle alongside the legal track is what bore fruit,” said Mannaa, a mainstay at the weeklong demonstrations at the site.

It was young people who drove the protests, villagers said. “Bring your coffee and come,” beckoned Sgaier in Instagram posts alongside his cousin. “We’re only going up to drink coffee, because that’s our land.”

“Not only the people of Majd al-Krum: Deir al-Asad, al-Bi’na, Sakhnin, Arrabeh … from the Naqab they came,” recalled Mannaa. Some left-leaning residents of nearby Jewish communities also turned up. “There was this incredible solidarity,” said Khalaily.

Hanan, a Palestinian Christian from a nearby village, said the outposts she read about in the occupied West Bank had felt far away – until Majd al-Krum. “I never saw the Arab community so united and really fighting for their lands,” she said.

Smotrich came to Majd al-Krum, a village long known for its political activism, to campaign with a police force and a water cannon. “The young people were hot-blooded and wanted to go out and confront him,” Khalaily said, but the local committees and political parties talked them down.

But the targeting continued. On September 18, police announced the arrest of a 32-year-old Majd al-Krum resident over alleged contact with a Lebanese agent. Smotrich seized on it, saying Galilee residents were “in the atmosphere of October 6”, a reference to the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel.

On August 27, Smotrich posted a plan promising one million more Jews and 40 new Jewish communities in the Galilee and al-Naqab, another area of Israel where many of the residents are Palestinian. His party then released an AI-generated video in which a West Bank Palestinian frantically warns a relative in the Galilee that “the Jews are coming” to “do to you what they did to us”.

Sgaier said he and his friends laughed at the absurdity of the video. Then they watched it come to life at al-Rus.

“He came here and said it clearly: ‘I want to Judaise the Galilee,’” said Khalaily. “Back in the day, they used to say, ‘we want to develop the Galilee.’ Today – the language is clear.”

Villagers believe the recent provocations are intended to create a pretext for making that happen, where Palestinian citizens hold rights that Palestinians under military occupation in the West Bank do not, making dispossession a harder proposition. “Building the outposts, they wanted to lead the people into a confrontation,” said Mannaa. “They want to impose a state of chaos because chaos benefits them.”

The settlers pointed to a grazing permit granted on the land of al-Rus from the quasi-governmental JNF. But according to Khalaily, the plot, about 8.4 dunams (roughly two acres), is half privately owned by his cousin, and half administered by the Israel Land Authority, which has long refused to partition it so the owner can tell which part is his.

“They chose Majd al-Krum because it’s hard to break,” said Mannaa, pointing to the village’s history of defiance since the Nakba in 1948, when many villagers were expelled from their homes. “If they break Majd al-Krum,” said Khaled Kewan, 27, a singer from the village, “[it’s] going to happen all over the Galilee”.

The JNF later said the “grazing” initiative would move to another plot about 500 metres away on land villagers consider theirs. But the village rejects any relocation, “even one tent”, Mannaa said.

Al Jazeera has reached out to the JNF, the Israeli police and the Israeli Finance Ministry for comment, but has yet to receive a response.

Whether Smotrich remains in power depends on the election results on Tuesday – where the Palestinian vote will likely figure prominently. Polls suggest neither of the main Zionist blocs can reach 61 seats without support from the Arab parties.

Turnout by Palestinian citizens of Israel has hovered between 45 and 65 percent in recent years. However, organisers believe the demographic’s turnout may hit 70 to 75 percent, a level last seen in 1999.

After the settlers’ attempts and provocations in Majd al-Krum, Mannaa boldly predicted the town “will go past 80 percent”.

Khalaily, a longtime boycotter who has only ever voted once, now urges turnout at every talk he gives. “These prominent racists who are there now have to be removed, even if just for a stage,” he said. He sees little difference between Netanyahu’s government and its likely replacement, “except that Smotrich and [far-right National Security Minister Itamar] Ben-Gvir won’t be in it”.

After October 7, fear kept Palestinian citizens away from demonstrating. “People got busy with other things,” said Khalaily. “Busy with fear, with making a living.” Crime in the town made it worse. “I’ll be sitting here at night and I hear the sound of shooting,” said Khalaily, who has children who witnessed three men murdered. “Nothing moves. It’s become normal.”

Palestinian citizens have more rights than those in the West Bank, leaving them caught between a system they oppose but must live in. “We here have the most to lose,” he said, “because we’re settled on our land and we stayed on it.”

As a result, many stayed quiet in recent years. “We left Gaza alone, left the West Bank alone, left Lebanon alone,” said Sgaier. “I said after that our time is coming.”

“I just didn’t expect it to come this early.”

However, after Smotrich’s rhetoric and the settlers’ local incursions, “the people who were indifferent about the elections, who didn’t want to take part or vote: the matter provoked them,” said Mannaa. “They know well what awaits us if this government returns to power.”

Some, like Sgaier, will still boycott. “What happened in Majd al-Krum, we solve it by going out [to] the street – not through the Knesset [parliament] and the laws,” said Sgaier, who sees little difference between the two Zionist political blocs. “They don’t want Palestinians here.”

Sgaier believes there was a real change where it counts: on the streets. During the protests at al-Rus, he saw people he never expected. “They are not politically engaged,” he said, “but they came, too”.

The settlers’ tents are gone, leaving only sparse remains and Hebrew graffiti proclaiming “the nation of Israel lives”. Nonetheless, villagers keep trekking up the mountain every day. Families barbecue there, and schoolchildren draw and play music.

During the weeklong protests, Khaled Kewan would leave al-Rus in the evenings to go to a recording studio. He and fellow musicians from the town made the song “ Ibn Bladi ”:

“Oh, land of mine, land of my ancestors!” he sings. “No matter how many walls they build across my country … I am a son of this land, a son of my own country.”

The inspiration was clear, but Kewan deliberately chose not to name Majd al-Krum explicitly. “Haifa’s my town too, Akka’s my town too, Sakhnin’s my town too, Arraba’s my town too … I love the whole homeland,” he said.

The settlers’ “Judaisation” efforts, he said, “are coming not just for Majd al-Krum, but for the whole Galilee.”

articles.title: Budget 2026: 'Surrey is a lovely place - but it can be stressful'
articles.summary: Ahead of the Budget, residents tell BBC Radio Surrey their experiences of the cost-of living crisis.
articles.body:
Surrey is one of the wealthiest parts of the country and, according to council papers, one of the largest net contributors to the UK economy after London.

But with average house prices at around £500,000 as well as high rents, it is also one of the most expensive places to live.

For many people in the county, there are huge cost-of-living pressures that are a struggle to deal with.

So as the Chancellor John Healey prepares to deliver his first budget on Wednesday, what kind of support are residents and businesses asking for?

Andy Hayward, the owner and head brewer at Thames Side Brewery, a pub and live music venue in Staines, told BBC Radio Surrey that working in hospitality "is tough generally... whether it's restaurants, pubs, breweries".

"We don't get many people coming in these days just for beer... they need something to come out for," he said.

"When I was growing up we used to go to the pub to meet and just chat and now it seems like people need a reason to go out, so the live music is really helping us."

Hayward said he would like the government to reduce business rates, cut VAT on hospitality and introduce measures so "the public have more money in their pocket".

Lucy, from Banstead, who has two children, says Surrey is a "lovely area to have kids in" but can be a "very stressful place to live" because it is "expensive".

She added she relies on places like Banstead Pantry , which is run by the charity Good Company, to "provide for my family".

"Once you've paid your essential bills, your energy, your rent, your fuel, things like that, you're left with nothing, and you want to be able to go out and spend money on (the) children and give them the things that they want and deserve and sometimes the money is just not there to do it now, which is hard," she told BBC Radio Surrey.

She wants ministers to prioritise lowering food prices.

Elmbridge has some of the highest housing costs and has seen a rise in the number of people living in poverty, with 68% of those being part of working households, according to the Walton Charity.

Jo Burton and James Stevenson, who both live in Hersham in the borough, have been sharing their cost-of-living experiences as part of a project the charity is running.

Burton said that food is "getting more expensive" and "school uniforms cost an absolute fortune and they don't need to".

She added: "Whatever system you're dealing with, it feels like a maze... you never really get anywhere and no one really properly helps you out."

'Understand what it's like on the ground'

Stevenson said that Surrey is "prohibitively expensive when you're in my financial situation".

"It's extremely difficult and every month we run out of money before the end of the month despite trying to keep our costs as low as possible and budgeting well," he said.

"We need to get the people at central government to actually understand what it's like on the ground."

Stevenson said ministers need to deal with energy costs and the costs of petrol and "take a much harder look at society and what the government can do".

An HM Treasury spokesperson said: "We know families are feeling the impact of higher prices, pushed up by conflicts overseas.

"The Chancellor is focused on giving households and businesses a bit of breathing space where we can.

"That's why we have removed VAT from electricity bills, capped bus fares in England at £2 in 2027, extended the 5p fuel duty cut, and frozen rail fares and prescription charges."

articles.title: Astley Hall in Chorley reopens after £400k restoration
articles.summary: Restored bedrooms show what life was like in 1852, while historic artwork returns to display.
articles.body:
A historic house in Lancashire has fully reopened following a £400,000 restoration.

Astley Hall, a Grade I-listed building in Chorley, welcomed visitors back into previously closed rooms after the final phase of a six-year restoration programme.

The work has allowed historic furniture and artwork to be back on display, while bedrooms have been furnished to reflect life at the hall more than 170 years ago.

Chorley MP Sir Lindsay Hoyle described Astley Hall as "one of Lancashire's best-kept secrets", admitting he was "totally biased".

The restoration focused on the West Wing, a section of the house built in about the 1570s for the local Charnock family.

The Stucco Bedroom and Cromwell Bedroom have been refreshed and furnished to reflect life in 1852, when Lady Susannah Hoghton lived at the hall, Chorley Council said.

Museum curator Amy Dearnaley said timber had begun to deteriorate before the restoration, with staff having to move furniture and other objects out of the way.

She also highlighted the Oak Bedroom, which contains an Elizabethan bed she described as one of the finest examples from its time.

She said the hall's kitchen display had previously been recreated using photographs from the early 1900s and historical inventories. Items had been sourced to match those pictured, down to a birdcage.

A Room of Reflection has also been newly arranged with artworks and objects from the Second World War.

Sir Lindsay said the hall, set within Astley Park near Chorley town centre, was an important part of the town's history and praised the council's continued investment in preserving it.

"It's a beautiful building, wonderful place, great for exhibitions, great for bringing people together, but it's the history of this as well," he said.

Chorley Council said the £400,000 project was funded by its own investment alongside £100,000 from the Wolfson Foundation, £34,000 from the government's UK Shared Prosperity Fund and £5,000 from the Friends of Astley Hall.

The council's deputy leader, Peter Wilson, said preserving the building was only part of the aim: it also needed to be open for people to enjoy and learn about its history.

Upcoming events include The Longest Yarn exhibition in November and Christmas activities at the hall.

articles.title: Budget hopes for first-time buyers struggling to save deposits
articles.summary: Aspiring homeowners say rent, rising costs and house prices are delaying plans to buy.
articles.body:
Pre Ramteke pays around £900 a month in rent before bills, but says saving enough for a deposit to buy her first home remains out of reach.

After moving to the UK from India in 2021, buying a home with her partner has proved difficult, due to rising house prices and the cost of living.

Her concerns come ahead of this week's Budget, when the government is expected to provide further details of its proposed Your First Home scheme, aimed at helping more first-time buyers onto the property ladder.

"Sometimes I do think that I'm trying to chase a dream that's going further and further away", she told the BBC.

The average interest rate on a new five-year fixed mortgage deal has hit 6% for the first time in three years, with house prices getting higher and higher.

Ramteke completed her studies in London and later moved to Rugby, hoping to put down roots.

"We know that if we buy a property, the instalments are going to be the exact same as the rent is right now. But the deposit is what is the biggest challenge for us," she said.

She estimates it could take three to four years to save enough for a deposit on a typical three-bedroom home.

Estate agent Zunara Tariq, of Oakmere Signature Homes, said affordability remained one of the biggest issues facing buyers.

She said: "It's a really tough time to save for a deposit. Even people who are on [big] salary jobs are finding it really hard.

"Affordability is a massive thing that we've seen at the moment, and cost of living and affordability work hand in hand."

While she welcomed government support, Tariq said no single scheme would work for everyone.

She said prices were continuing to rise and lenders were more cautious.

"Any support available is positive support in the right direction, but it may not always be practical and it isn't always suitable for every first-time buyer," she added.

Tyne Steele, a self-employed electrician who is also saving for his first home, said renting while trying to build up a deposit was a challenge.

He rents a home with his partner and said that while sharing costs helped, unexpected bills could quickly eat into savings.

He said: "It is hard to save. If your car breaks down, it could be £1,000 gone out of that savings pot.

"[The] cost of living, that needs to be addressed."

He welcomed incentives such as the Lifetime ISA, but said tackling wider financial pressures should remain a priority.

"I'd rather owe one person money to the bank, [rather] than the government and the bank," he added.

The government has said its proposed Your First Home scheme would help tackle the deposit barrier facing aspiring homeowners and support more people into home ownership.

The scheme is expected to offer 2.5% deposits alongside government-backed equity loans for eligible first-time buyers purchasing new-build homes.

Tariq said buyers should seek professional advice and understand all their options before making such a significant purchase.

"Every single buyer has a different experience," she said.

"You're only a first-time buyer once, so make sure you're fully educated before you buy anything."

articles.title: Ofcom: Sports 'geo-blocking' can't be stopped says regulator
articles.summary: The UK media regulator has said the geo-blocking of Irish sporting events in Northern Ireland could get worse.
articles.body:
The UK media regulator, Ofcom, has concluded that the "geo-blocking" of Irish sporting events in Northern Ireland is currently an insoluble problem and may get worse.

Geo-blocking refers to the restriction of access to streamed content based on a viewer's geographical location.

It means that sporting events on RTÉ and other Irish channels are frequently unavailable to viewers in Northern Ireland.

Ofcom said it doesn't have the power to stop it and that there are no technical measures which offer "a complete, low-cost and universally applicable solution".

It added that as more TV output is delivered via streaming services it will impact a "growing part of television consumption".

It had been asked to review the issue by Stormont's economy minister Caoimhe Archibald having last looked at it in 2015.

The regulator said two constraints continue to drive geo-blocking: "Territorial content rights, particularly for major sport, and the limitations of using internet protocol (IP) addresses to establish that a viewer is in Northern Ireland."

It said it has "no power to require a rights holder to license content on an all-island basis".

It is also "not aware of any regulatory mechanism that would allow it to require an Internet Service Provider (ISP) to reserve IP addresses for Northern Ireland."

'The additional cost may be disproportionate'

RTÉ and TG4 try to buy sports rights on an all-island basis but Ofcom says that in practical terms that is rarely possible.

It said: "In many cases international sporting organisations and their agents sell separate packages for the UK and the Republic of Ireland.

"Northern Ireland is normally included within the UK package.

"Bespoke arrangements for NI are not always available commercially. Where an alternative arrangement is available, the additional cost may be disproportionate for relatively small public service broadcasters."

In addition, it said the way in which IP addresses are currently managed means geolocation databases cannot reliably distinguish a Northern Ireland user from one in Great Britain.

Ofcom has suggested that a first step to any solution would be for the British and Irish governments to review their 2010 Memorandum of Understanding which covered cross-border access to digital terrestrial TV.

That agreement was about making sure BBC channels could be easily received in the Republic and RTÉ/TG4 in Northern Ireland via terrestrial signals.

Ofcom said a review could assess whether its scope should cover IP-delivered services as well as digital terrestrial TV.

The economy minister said the geo-blocking of RTÉ content is "completely unacceptable and must be brought to an end".

She has asked the governments to start the review suggested by Ofcom.

"I have written again to the British and Irish governments to seek their engagement and cooperation on resolving this issue once and for all," she said.

articles.title: Budget hopes as South West hospitality faces 'uphill battle'
articles.summary: Tourism leaders warn the government further taxation in the Budget will "hinder growth".
articles.body:
Tourism and hospitality leaders have warned the government any further taxation or financial pressures in the upcoming Budget would "hinder growth".

Katie Warren, the chair of the Cornwall Visitors Alliance, said the sector was watching "with absolutely bated breath".

Many businesses in Devon and Cornwall have also called for the Chancellor John Healey to reverse last year's changes to National Insurance contributions .

Healey will deliver his first Budget on Wednesday, but has refused to rule out tax increases after acknowledging government borrowing costs are at "historic highs".

Warren has run a self-catering holiday let business in Falmouth, Cornwall, for 15 years, said: "We would like to see cuts to VAT, cuts to small business rates and a look back at the National Insurance contributions system."

A rise in employer's National Insurance was announced in Labour's first Budget in 2024 and took effect in April 2025.

Warren said it had been "absolutely diabolical for the sector" and "tens of thousands of jobs have been cut across the UK since the changes came in".

"Businesses have had to close because they could not meet those overheads along with the constant rise in operational costs," she added.

In Newquay, Cornwall, Chris Thomson is the owner and founder of 10 Over Surf Shop, that also hosts a café, barbers and marketing agency.

He said it was "tough" starting a small business and "it constantly feels like an uphill battle".

He said: "From our perspective on hospitality, it'd be amazing to see the VAT rate reduced.

"Simply because the highest cost for hospitality is staff wages and you can't reclaim VAT against that.

"So lowering the VAT rate to 10% would just give us a bit more margin to improve the business and invest in our team."

At the River Dart Country Park, near Ashburton in Devon, general manager Roger Sell said they employed about 100 staff depending on the season, with about 30% under the age of 18.

Sell, who is also chairman for the Devon Association of Tourist Attractions, said he wanted to see measures to encourage youth employment in the Budget.

"Employment in our sector is huge and we're in the customer service business, so we have to employ in the right way, and we have to do a lot of training with our staff.

"So anything that is putting a restriction on us employing, like the National Insurance contributions, is having a massive effect in the tourism sector," he said.

articles.title: Theatre Royal Wakefield expansion plans lodged
articles.summary: Trust aims to secure the future of Theatre Royal Wakefield as a 'vital heritage and cultural asset'.
articles.body:
Plans for a major extension and refurbishment of Theatre Royal Wakefield have been submitted to the council.

The proposals aim to modernise the Grade II* listed venue while protecting its historic character and improving accessibility.

Changes would include a new second-floor extension, upgraded audience facilities and improvements to the auditorium.

The trust behind the theatre said the work would help secure its future as a "vital heritage and cultural asset".

Documents lodged with Wakefield Council by Wakefield Theatre Trust include proposals for a new extension above the building's west wing on Drury Lane.

The scheme would create additional backstage facilities, alongside a new lift and staircase to improve access throughout the venue.

Internal alterations are also planned, including a new bar, dressing room, studio space and toilets.

The theatre's auditorium would be upgraded with new lighting and improved seating in the stalls and dress circle. Capacity would increase from 493 to 510.

A planning statement submitted on behalf of the trust said the 132-year-old building faced a backlog of repair and conservation work.

It said the improvements were needed to provide better access, modern facilities and new opportunities to generate income, helping ensure the long-term future of the theatre.

The venue was built in 1894 as the Wakefield Opera House and was designed by renowned theatre architect Frank Matcham. It is believed to be the smallest surviving theatre designed by him.

After closing as a theatre in 1954, the building was used as a cinema and later as a bingo hall before being bought by a trust in 1981. It reopened as a theatre in 1986.

Katie Town, chief executive of Wakefield Theatre Trust, said: "Safeguarding the building's architectural and historic significance is central to the project."

She said the plans would help secure the theatre's future as a working professional venue while reducing its carbon footprint.

She said the redesign must "enhance its function and ensure its sustainability so it can serve as one of Wakefield's cultural cornerstones for many years to come".

The Local Democracy Reporting Service said the application followed discussions with the council and Historic England.

articles.title: A Court of Splintered Harmony: Fans revel in midnight release at Carrickfergus event
articles.summary: About 40 fans of A Court of Thorns and Roses series celebrated at a "lock-in" event in Carrickfergus.
articles.body:
Torrential rain and high winds may not be what many would consider fantastical.

But it didn't stop about 30 hardcore fans turning out for the latest release of author Sarah J Maas’ romantasy series, A Court of Splintered Harmony, in Carrickfergus, County Antrim.

The sixth book in Maas's multi-million book selling series, A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR), was released at midnight on Tuesday after a five-year wait.

On Monday evening, a midnight release event was held in The Secret Bookshelf, an independent bookshop just off the town's main street.

Friends Katie Mccabrey and Amy Savage were among those who went along to try and get one of the first copies when the embargo broke.

Like many others, Katie and Amy love reading books as a way to unwind from the stresses and pressures of every day life.

"I just love reading these kinds of fantasy books because the real world is a little bit terrible and I love to escape into a fantasyland of fairies and anything other worldly," Amy says.

"We're all here tonight because we all share just needing to escape from everyday life in common and this is a great way to do it," Katie adds.

Among the activities lined up at The Secret Bookshelf to distract excited fans from clock-watching are felting, friendship bracelet making and a dedicated fan-chat area for readers to discuss their theories.

Some attending opt for comfy clothing, sporting pyjamas and slippers as they waited for the midnight drop.

The wait has almost been too much for Katie.

"I couldn't sleep, I've been so excited - I've been hyped up for two weeks straight," she says.

"I'm actually halfway through another book that I couldn't pay attention to because I've been so busy thinking about the characters from ACOTAR," Amy jokes.

"So I'm going to have to go back and re-read the book that I'm 300 pages deep in because I've been so busy and so excited for this new launch."

For those whose social media algorithms do not revolve around "BookTok", the literary discussion side of TikTok, A Court of Thorns and Roses - or ACOTAR for short - is a fantasy romance series, which gets its name from the first book.

It's set in the fictional world of Prythian, and without spoiling the now six-book series, fans have flocked to the story in their droves to read about the protagonist's dealings with love and the fae.

Maas is also credited with fuelling interest in the romantasy genre, which has skyrocketed in popularity due to its discussion on social media.

There have been five books published so far:

Maas announced the series' latest installment, A Court of Splintered Harmony, back in March .

And fans won't have to wait long for the follow-up, with the seventh book, A Court of Forgotten Melody, due to be released on 12 January 2027.

David Jeroen and Sami Patrick are hard to miss amongst the stacked shelves in The Secret Bookshelf - they've donned their finest mythical attire for the evening, with crowns and elf ears included.

The pair's love of reading prompted them to start an Instagram account dedicated to books, and they're spending their two-year "bookiversary" in an apt place.

And Sami's excited to spend the night talking about one of her favourite genres with likeminded people.

"I've always been a fantasy reader and it's just escapism really," she says.

"I think it's all about escaping reality and going into a different world and dimension where you get to live through another character and experience new things that you wouldn't be able to in real life," he adds.

"You can't ride a dragon in real life so you can read about it."

While the evening will conclude with the newest ACOTAR release, Sami says the five-year wait has led her to some of Maas's other series, which she prefers.

Bookshops should 'foster' love for reading

Monday's midnight release event is the brainchild of Jo Zebedee, who runs The Secret Bookshelf alongside her husband, Chris.

Harkening back to her time helping to run the midnight launches of the Harry Potter books, Jo decided to bring the same magic for fans of the much loved romantasy series.

"We are a big fantasy shop, I'm a fantasy, sci-fi writer so it's in my blood, so we very much celebrate the world's that sometime can be difficult to find a space in mainstream books," she explains.

"There's something around the excitement of books and just that whole vibe of here's something to really celebrate.. we just wanted to bring that all together to make a fun night."

Jo enlisted the help of not only local crafters for the event, but local businesses who gifted attendees treats for the late night.

She thinks its the place of independent bookshops, like hers, to foster the excitement amongst young people for reading.

"I think events is when a bookshop comes to life," she says.

"It's about a love of books and tonight is just such a love of books."

articles.body: Facebook-parent company Meta announced on Monday (October ) that it plans to raise up to $95 billion in its largest-ever equity fundraising effort, seeking fresh capital to fuel its massive artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure expansion without diluting CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s voting control. articles.title: US, EU and 30 countries warn of famine risk in Sudan, call for aid
articles.summary: Countries also urge Sudan’s warring parties to ‘lift all impediments on humanitarian assistance’.
articles.body:
The United States, the European Union and 30 countries have warned of an “alarming deterioration” in food security in Sudan, calling for “urgent action” to prevent famine in the African country.

In a joint statement released by the US State Department on Monday, the signatories called on the groups fighting Sudan’s civil war “to lift all impediments on humanitarian assistance”.

The signatories included Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, France, Germany and the European Commissioner ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠for equality, preparedness and crisis management.

“Sudan is experiencing an alarming deterioration in its food security. The risk of famine in the coming months, as warned by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, needs urgent action,” the statement said. “The parties to the conflict bear primary responsibility for alleviating the suffering of the Sudanese people.”

Sudan’s army has been fighting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces since April 2023, when a dispute over how to integrate the two forces erupted into clashes in the capital, Khartoum. The war has killed tens of thousands of people, displaced more than 13 million, and created the world’s largest hunger and displacement crises.

In June, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a United Nations-backed hunger monitor known as the IPC, said 5.1 million people in Sudan faced severe hunger.

Farmers have struggled to harvest crops since the war began, and the IPC said a drought linked to El Nino had driven up food prices and reduced supplies this year.

Without immediate action, the joint statement warned, “the number of children suffering from severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825,000.”

The signatories urged the warring parties to allow humanitarian operations through all routes across front lines and borders, including air access to the region of Darfur. They also called on the parties to “sustain presence and protection of humanitarian personnel” throughout Sudan and to refrain from hitting civilian infrastructure.

“In the face of a potential famine, we call on all members of the international community to urgently scale up funding in response to increased needs and support efforts to ensure assistance reaches those most in need,” the statement said.

Besides the US, Australia and Canada, the statement was signed by 28 European countries.

Last month, the State Department ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠said that neither the Sudanese army nor the RSF “represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan”.

articles.title: An Indiana man threw rocks at his ex-wife's home and later set her fence on fire; despite guilty pleas, an October 23 appeals court overturned $15,017.50 in restitution orders because they were added after sentencing
articles.summary: A guilty plea does not give a court unlimited authority to change a sentence after it has been finalised.
articles.body: A guilty plea does not give a court unlimited authority to change a sentence after it has been finalised. An Indiana man who admitted to damaging his ex-wife’s property has won an appeal against restitution orders totalling $15,017.50, after a court found that the trial judge lacked the authority to impose the payments months after sentencing.According to an October 23 memorandum decision by the Indiana Court of Appeals, available on Justia, the original sentencing orders did not require restitution or reserve the issue for later consideration. The appellate court reversed the orders and instructed the trial court to remove the unauthorised amounts from the relevant sentencing records, while leaving the man’s guilty pleas and convictions undisturbed.Rocks thrown at ex-wife’s home followed by fence arsonThe case involved David McDonald, who faced criminal charges after two separate incidents involving his ex-wife’s property in 2025. In February that year, McDonald went to his ex-wife’s home and threw two rocks at the house. An active protective order prohibited him from contacting her. Following the incident, the State charged him with Class B misdemeanour criminal mischief.Later in 2025, McDonald returned to the property, poured gasoline on part of his ex-wife’s wooden fence and set it on fire. The incident led to a Level 6 felony arson charge, along with other charges. McDonald was also facing a separate Level 6 felony theft case involving his employer. He subsequently entered into a single plea agreement covering these and several other pending cases. Under the agreement, he pleaded guilty to criminal mischief and arson in the cases involving his ex-wife, as well as theft in the separate case involving his employer.Plea agreement left restitution open in only one caseThe dispute centred on what the plea agreement allowed the trial court to decide after sentencing. According to the appellate decision, the agreement expressly left the amount of restitution in the theft case open for determination at a later hearing. It did not include a provision requiring McDonald to pay restitution to his ex-wife in the criminal mischief and arson cases.At the sentencing hearing, the State attempted to present evidence concerning restitution in the theft case. However, because McDonald’s former employer was not present, the trial court deferred the matter to a later hearing and proceeded to sentence him on the charges covered by the agreement. On February 4, 2026, the court entered sentencing orders in the criminal mischief and arson cases. Neither order mentioned restitution, and neither stated that the court was retaining authority to decide the issue later.The restitution question returned before the trial court on May 6, when a hearing was scheduled in the separate theft case. During the proceedings, the prosecution sought to address restitution for the damage to McDonald’s ex-wife’s property as well. McDonald’s defence objected, arguing that the hearing was scheduled only for the theft case and that the plea agreement did not leave restitution open in the other cases. The trial court nevertheless proceeded to consider the claims.Trial court ordered $15,017.50 in paymentsFollowing the May hearing, the trial court ordered McDonald to pay his ex-wife $3,760 for the criminal mischief case and $11,257.50 for the arson case. Together, the two orders totalled $15,017.50. The trial court later amended the arson sentencing order following a June 3 hearing on McDonald’s motion to correct his credit time. However, the amended order also included the $3,760 restitution amount in its monetary obligations section.McDonald challenged the restitution orders before the Indiana Court of Appeals, arguing that the trial court had already entered final judgments in the criminal mischief and arson cases and therefore lacked the authority to add restitution afterwards. The State argued that the trial court had indicated during the earlier proceedings that restitution would be addressed later. The appellate court rejected that position, noting that the discussion at sentencing concerned restitution for McDonald’s employer in the theft case, not payments to his ex-wife.Appeals court reverses restitution ordersThe Indiana Court of Appeals concluded that the trial court lacked the authority to impose restitution in the criminal mischief and arson cases after entering final sentencing orders. The judges explained that restitution forms part of a criminal sentence and that a trial court cannot ordinarily modify a sentence without continuing authority provided by the judgment, a statute or a rule. In McDonald’s case, the original sentencing orders did not reserve the restitution issue, and the plea agreement contemplated restitution only in the theft case.The appellate court also clarified that the agreement’s reference to an open plea did not give the trial court unrestricted discretion. The only unresolved matters were the amount of restitution in the theft case and where McDonald would serve 365 days of his sentence. The court therefore reversed the restitution orders and remanded the cases with instructions to vacate the $3,760 criminal mischief order and the $11,257.50 arson order. It also directed the trial court to amend the arson sentencing record to remove the $3,760 amount from the monetary obligations section.The decision did not overturn McDonald’s guilty pleas or convictions for criminal mischief and arson. It addressed the trial court’s authority to impose the additional payments after sentencing. The October 23 ruling was issued as a memorandum decision and, under Indiana Appellate Rule 65(D), is not binding precedent for any court. articles.title: Ranking England's Ballon d'Or winners - how does Kane compare?
articles.summary: From Stanley Matthews to Harry Kane, how do England's Ballon d'Or winners rank?
articles.body:
English Ballon d'Or winners have been few and far between. Triumphs to be treasured, names never to be forgotten.

Harry Kane, England's great talisman and captain, is the first to claim football's grandest individual accolade in 25 years after a sensational campaign in Bayern Munich colours - and only the fifth Englishman to ever do so.

Before him Michael Owen, in 2001, was the first Three Lions star to take it since Kevin Keegan's successive triumphs 22 years earlier.

England World Cup winner Bobby Charlton did it in 1966, and that came after Stanley Matthews won the inaugural prize a decade earlier - handed what began life as the European Footballer of the Year award in 1956.

Others have come close - Billy Wright, Bobby Moore, Gary Lineker, David Beckham and Frank Lampard are all among the runners-up. Lucy Bronze, in 2019, and Beth Mead, 2022, also more recently finished second.

Of course, the award has gradually evolved into the global behemoth it is today.

The caveat with those earlier winners is that it was not a worldwide prize - until 1995 it was only open to European players, and only in 2007 did it expand to include all players from all clubs across the world.

However, that does not detract from the award-winning performances these stars produced - each enjoyed prize-worthy campaigns that caught voters' eyes across Europe and the world.

But who among the five to have held the coveted prize is England's greatest Ballon d'Or winner?

We won't hold it against Michael Owen for suggesting he didn't know what the Ballon d'Or was when Gerard Houllier first rang to announce he'd won it.

And, in fairness, the then 22-year-old swotted up sufficiently by the time he received the award, reeling off a list of previous winners.

Owen in those days, even after his initial hamstring struggles, was explosive, electric - searing pace and acceleration complemented by the most ruthless of finishes. He became a renowned goalscorer in his teenage years and, by 2001, was one of the most sought-after youngsters in world football.

Owen's Ballon d'Or-winning year was one of iconic moments. He helped Liverpool to a treble, clinching the League Cup on penalties before beating Arsenal in the FA Cup final - Owen scored twice late on to turn the game in Liverpool's favour.

The leveller was an acrobatic and clinically taken strike inside the Arsenal box, the winner a devastating break in which the prolific striker darted away from Lee Dixon and Tony Adams before slotting past David Seaman with his left foot.

The forward then set up two of the goals as Houllier's side beat Alaves 5-4 in extra time in the Uefa Cup final, having earlier in the competition scored a famous double against Roma at the Stadio Olimpico that carried the Reds through.

He finished the season as Liverpool's top goalscorer with 24 in all competitions. Owen's most iconic performance that year, however, came for England against Germany, scoring a famous hat-trick in Munich.

Injuries meant Owen never maintained that peak for as long as he would have hoped. Indeed, only Brazilian great Ronaldo claimed a Ballon d'Or at a more tender age.

Sir Stanley Matthews, first and oldest winner of the Ballon d'Or - a prize then decided by voters from 16 countries.

Twelve of the panel put the Blackpool winger on their ballot, with six placing him first - beating Alfredo di Stefano and Raymond Kopa, who competed in the inaugural European Cup final for Real Madrid and Reims, respectively. That alone shows how revered Matthews was.

Matthews, two months shy of his 42nd birthday when he received the award, led Blackpool to second in the English top flight. This was behind Manchester United's Busby Babes that season, though voters were likely influenced by his performance in the FA Cup final three years earlier. Then, the Tangerines beat Bolton 4-3 in a match dubbed the 'Matthews Final' and broadcast in cinemas.

In an era where following the game often came largely via radio and newspaper reports, Matthews' mythical status drew fans to stadiums in huge numbers, with curious onlookers keen for a glimpse of his magic whenever Blackpool came to town. He dazzled for England, too.

Matthews was born during the First World War and would remarkably continue playing for another nine years after his award, retiring aged 50. His longevity no doubt was a factor, but should not take away from his continued brilliance.

Matthews was famous the world over, lauded by fellow stars for his creativity and ingenuity at a time where greatness did not boil down to individual stats. A creator rather than a scorer.

He was innovative, too. Nicknamed 'The Wizard of the Dribble', he would perform stretching and breathing exercises, do extra training and take care of his diet - fasting and not drinking alcohol.

Most poignantly, he was one of football's great entertainers, described by Ballon d'Or founder Gabriel Hanot - who was thought to have preferred Di Stefano - as the sport's Charlie Chaplin.

Matthews was adored by a generation, an outside right who became an icon. He received the award in the modest surroundings of Blackpool Town Hall, a low-key affair but one that cemented his legacy.

Now, Harry Kane has produced one of the most sensational individual campaigns on record. You could argue that should place him higher, but those above him on this list have done some heavy lifting, too.

Looking at his output from the beginning of the 2025-26 season to the end of this summer's World Cup, the evaluation period for this year's award, Kane has delivered the most goals for club and country by any player in Europe's top five leagues since Lionel Messi's astonishing 2011-12 return.

The England skipper netted 61 times in 51 outings across all competitions for Bayern, winning a German league and cup double while also becoming the fastest player to hit a century of Bundesliga goals.

He also scored 12 times for his country, with six of those coming during England's run to the World Cup semi-finals.

The argument, of course, is that Kane is playing for a dominant Bayern side in a league they are heavy favourites to win each year.

The counter is the 33-year-old has redefined the centre-forward role - his incredible passing range and hold-up play making him an all-round playmaker.

Kane has been developing and maturing into one of England's all-time greats ever since those early loan spells at Leyton Orient and Millwall. His Premier League output for Tottenham was phenomenal season upon season, gradually adding assists to a prolific goal output.

In Munich, especially last season, Kane has just taken that to another level.

2. Bobby Charlton, Manchester United, 1966

The question mark hanging over those winners pre-1995, when the award opened beyond European players, or even before 2007, when it became truly global, is whether there was a more worthy recipient sitting outside the current criteria.

Some may argue Igor Belanov was slightly upstaged by Diego Maradona in 1986, for example.

But 20 years earlier, few could dismiss the credentials of a man who pioneered the Three Lions' first and only World Cup triumph, Manchester United's Bobby Charlton.

A survivor of the Munich Air Disaster in 1958, Charlton and United went on to win the FA Cup in 1963 and English top flight two years later. By 1966, at the age of 28, Charlton was in his prime, heading into the World Cup on the back of 16 top-flight goals from midfield for United that season.

Not only was he at the heart of that United side, who reached the European Cup semi-finals, he was the man England boss Alf Ramsey decided to build his team around for a first World Cup on home soil.

After an opening goalless draw with Uruguay, Charlton gave England's campaign lift-off with a scampering run from the halfway line followed by a trademark strike from distance that was still rising when it crashed into the corner of the Wembley net.

Charlton helped carry the hosts to the semi-finals, where he scored twice as England knocked out Euesbio's Portugal, before he and West Germany's Franz Beckenbauer tussled in the final as England won 4-2 in extra time.

Benfica's Eusebio finished second to Charlton in the Ballon d'Or rankings that year and Bayern Munich's Beckenbauer was third, with Charlton's World Cup performances showcasing not only his knack for a goal, passing range and poise, but also his selflessness. A true team player.

It was a fruitful era for individual success at Old Trafford. Scotland's Denis Law won the Ballon d'Or two years earlier and Northern Ireland's George Best scooped the prize in 1968 as United won the European Cup.

Charlton finished second in successive years after his triumph. But his pivotal role in England's World Cup triumph earns him the runner-up spot on this list.

When it comes to Ballon d'Or-winning credentials, it had to be the only Englishman to do it twice.

Kevin Keegan scored 20 times as Liverpool won the European Cup and English First Division in 1977, and were a whisker away from completing the Treble - losing the FA Cup final to Manchester United. He also finished as Ballon d'Or runner-up to Borussia Monchengladbach's Danish star Allan Simonsen.

Keegan followed Simonsen to Germany by the time the award was announced, joining Cup Winners' Cup holders Hamburg on a lucrative deal, though they were hammered by his former side in the European Super Cup - and Keegan endured a slow start to Bundesliga life that was not helped by an eight-week suspension for punching someone in a friendly during the winter break.

Keegan soon settled but his first season was nothing spectacular. Instead 'Mighty Mouse' made a flying start to the new campaign - one in which Hamburg would become Bundesliga champions for the first time.

He also produced some impressive individual displays for England, even though the Three Lions missed out on that summer's World Cup, scoring against Brazil in a friendly and twice against Denmark in September.

Keegan's form was timely. He arguably deserved to win the Ballon d'Or a year earlier, which perhaps lingered in voters' minds, making 22 of the 26 ballot papers and ranking top on nine to finish above Barcelona's Austrian star Hans Krankl.

Keegan continued to flourish after Christmas to finish with 17 top-flight goals, including 11 in 12 games during the run-in. But it was more than just the goals, with Keegan a scampering, relentlessly creative presence.

The fluid, attacking HSV were in the midst of storming their way to a European Cup final when Keegan was named Europe's best player for a second successive year on Christmas Day 1979, this time being named top by 18 of the 26 voters.

The permed Keegan was the continent's biggest star and a cultural icon, too.

Hamburg would lose the European Cup final to Nottingham Forest at the Bernabeu, Keegan's last game before leaving for Southampton.

But he stands alone as the only British player to win two Ballon d'Or awards - at the time, only Johan Cruyff had matched his feat of going back-to-back - and that, of course, makes him England's greatest recipient.
